HIGH Accessibility CONFIRMED · 95% TRIVIAL fix

Interactive controls have no accessible name

12 pages 22 occurrences WCAG 2.1 — 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value priority 175

1 visible interactive element(s) expose no accessible name.

How we know measured evidence
Unnamed controls 1 Accessible-name computation
div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ul > li > a <a> DOM extraction
Why this matters interpretation

These are almost always icon-only controls — a hamburger menu, a close button, a search icon — where the icon is rendered as an SVG or a background image with no text alternative. Sighted users read the icon; assistive technology has nothing to read.

Impact: A screen reader announces these as "button" or "link" with no name. In a page with several, the user cannot distinguish between them at all.

Recommended fix trivial effort

Add `aria-label` describing the action ("Close dialog", "Open navigation menu", "Search"), or include visually-hidden text inside the control. For SVG icons, `<title>` inside the SVG plus `role="img"` also works.

<html> element must have a lang attribute

13 pages 13 occurrences WCAG 2.1 — 3.1.1 priority 160

Ensure every HTML document has a lang attribute

How we know measured evidence
axe rule html-has-lang axe-core
Impact serious axe-core
Failing elements on this page 1 axe-core
WCAG criteria 3.1.1 axe-core rule tags
Why this matters interpretation

This is a failure of WCAG success criterion 3.1.1. Ensure every HTML document has a lang attribute Users relying on assistive technology are affected directly; the failure is invisible to sighted mouse users, which is why it persists.

Impact: This blocks or seriously degrades use of the page for people relying on assistive technology.

Recommended fix small effort

Add a `lang` attribute to the `<html>` element so screen readers select the correct pronunciation rules.

Reference: https://dequeuniversity.com/rules/axe/4.13/html-has-lang?application=axeAPI

HIGH Accessibility CONFIRMED · 95% SMALL fix

Elements must meet minimum color contrast ratio thresholds

12 pages 86 occurrences WCAG 2.1 — 1.4.3 priority 157

Ensure the contrast between foreground and background colors meets WCAG 2 AA minimum contrast ratio thresholds

How we know measured evidence
axe rule color-contrast axe-core
Impact serious axe-core
Failing elements on this page 7 axe-core
WCAG criteria 1.4.3 axe-core rule tags
Why this matters interpretation

This is a failure of WCAG success criterion 1.4.3. Ensure the contrast between foreground and background colors meets WCAG 2 AA minimum contrast ratio thresholds Users relying on assistive technology are affected directly; the failure is invisible to sighted mouse users, which is why it persists.

Impact: Users with low vision, colour vision deficiency, or anyone reading on a phone in daylight cannot reliably read this text.

Recommended fix small effort

Increase the contrast between the text and its background to at least 4.5:1 for body text (3:1 for text at 18pt/14pt-bold or larger). Adjusting the text colour is usually less disruptive than changing the background.

Technical detail 
Rule: color-contrast (serious impact)
Reference: https://dequeuniversity.com/rules/axe/4.13/color-contrast?application=axeAPI

HIGH Accessibility CONFIRMED · 95% SMALL fix

Links must have discernible text

12 pages 22 occurrences WCAG 2.1 — 2.4.4, 4.1.2 priority 157

Ensure links have discernible text

How we know measured evidence
axe rule link-name axe-core
Impact serious axe-core
Failing elements on this page 1 axe-core
WCAG criteria 2.4.4, 4.1.2 axe-core rule tags
Why this matters interpretation

This is a failure of WCAG success criterion 2.4.4, 4.1.2. Ensure links have discernible text Users relying on assistive technology are affected directly; the failure is invisible to sighted mouse users, which is why it persists.

Impact: The control announces with no name, so a screen reader user has no way to know what activating it will do. In a list of links this makes the page unnavigable.

Recommended fix small effort

Give the link discernible text. Where the link is an icon, add `aria-label` or visually-hidden text — a link that announces as "link" with no name is unusable by screen reader.

Technical detail 
Rule: link-name (serious impact)
Reference: https://dequeuniversity.com/rules/axe/4.13/link-name?application=axeAPI

Why this matters interpretation

On a slow 4G connection (~1.6 Mbps) this payload alone takes roughly 14.4 seconds to transfer, before any parsing or rendering. image accounts for 2.32 MB — 83% of the total — so that is where the leverage is.

Impact: Longer load times on every connection, and materially longer on mobile networks. Users on metered connections also pay for these bytes directly.

Recommended fix medium effort

Serve images in AVIF/WebP at the dimensions they are displayed at, and use responsive `srcset` so mobile devices do not download desktop-sized assets. Enable Brotli compression at the edge for all text-based resources if it is not already active.

Page has no viewport meta tag

1 page 1 occurrence WCAG 2.1 — 1.4.10 Reflow priority 96

No `<meta name="viewport">` was found, so mobile browsers will render the page at desktop width and scale it down.

How we know measured evidence
Viewport meta (absent) DOM extraction
Why this matters interpretation

Without a viewport declaration, mobile browsers assume a 980px-wide desktop layout and zoom out to fit. Text becomes unreadably small and every tap target shrinks proportionally. Search engines also treat the page as not mobile-friendly, which affects mobile ranking.

Impact: The site is effectively unusable on phones without pinch-zooming, and is penalised in mobile search.

Recommended fix trivial effort

Add `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` to the document head.

Document has no lang attribute

13 pages 13 occurrences WCAG 2.1 — 3.1.1 Language of Page priority 89

The `<html>` element has no `lang` attribute.

How we know measured evidence
html[lang] (absent) DOM extraction
Why this matters interpretation

Screen readers use the document language to choose a pronunciation model. Without it they fall back to the user's system language, so English content may be read with, say, German phonetics — technically audible but very hard to follow.

Impact: Screen reader output can be mispronounced to the point of being unintelligible. Also affects browser translation prompts.

Recommended fix trivial effort

Add the correct BCP 47 tag, e.g. `<html lang="en">` or `<html lang="en-GB">`.

No Content-Security-Policy header

13 pages 13 occurrences OWASP Secure Headers Project priority 80

The `content-security-policy` response header is not set.

How we know measured evidence
Header content-security-policy HTTP response headers
Present no HTTP response headers
Why this matters interpretation

CSP is the primary defence against cross-site scripting. It tells the browser which sources are allowed to execute script, so that even if an attacker manages to inject a `<script>` tag, the browser refuses to run it. Without a policy, any successful injection executes with full privileges.

Impact: This is a missing defence-in-depth control rather than an exploitable vulnerability on its own. It increases the damage another flaw could do.

Recommended fix small effort

Deploy a Content-Security-Policy. Start in report-only mode (`Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`) with a collection endpoint so you can see what would break before enforcing, then tighten toward `default-src 'self'` with explicit allowances.

No Strict-Transport-Security header

13 pages 13 occurrences OWASP Secure Headers Project priority 80

The `strict-transport-security` response header is not set.

How we know measured evidence
Header strict-transport-security HTTP response headers
Present no HTTP response headers
Why this matters interpretation

HSTS instructs the browser to use HTTPS for this host for a stated period, without waiting for a redirect. It closes the window in which a first plain-http request can be intercepted and downgraded — the classic coffee-shop attack.

Impact: This is a missing defence-in-depth control rather than an exploitable vulnerability on its own. It increases the damage another flaw could do.

Recommended fix small effort

Add `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains`. Roll out with a short max-age first and confirm every subdomain serves HTTPS correctly before extending it, because the directive is not easily reversible in browsers that have cached it.

146 static assets lack a long cache lifetime

12 pages 12 occurrences priority 78

146 first-party static resources (2.79 MB) are served without an effective Cache-Control lifetime.

How we know measured evidence
Assets affected 146 Response headers
Bytes re-downloaded per visit 2.79 MB Chromium network stack
/css/bootstrap.min.css (no Cache-Control) Response headers
/css/jquery-ui.css (no Cache-Control) Response headers
/css/lc_lightbox.css (no Cache-Control) Response headers
/css/aos.css (no Cache-Control) Response headers
/css/style.css (no Cache-Control) Response headers
Why this matters interpretation

Without a long `max-age`, the browser must revalidate or re-download these assets on every visit. For fingerprinted build outputs — filenames containing a content hash — this is pure waste: the content can never change under a given URL, so it is safe to cache indefinitely.

Impact: Repeat visitors re-download assets that have not changed, making the second visit almost as slow as the first and consuming bandwidth unnecessarily.

Recommended fix small effort

Serve fingerprinted assets with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`. For assets whose URL is stable across deploys, use a shorter max-age with `stale-while-revalidate` so the browser can serve instantly while refreshing in the background.

Interactive targets are too small

3 pages 9 occurrences WCAG 2.2 — 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) priority 55

Interactive target is 156×21px, below the 24×24px minimum.

How we know measured evidence
Instances on this page 4 In-page geometry measurement
Viewport 1440×900 (desktop) Probe configuration
width 156 px getBoundingClientRect
height 21 px getBoundingClientRect
minimum 24 px getBoundingClientRect
Why this matters interpretation

WCAG 2.2 sets a 24×24 CSS pixel minimum for pointer targets. Below that, users with motor impairments, larger fingers, or an unsteady grip miss the target repeatedly. The measurement here is of the rendered box, so it accounts for padding.

Impact: Mis-taps and repeated attempts, particularly on touch devices and for users with reduced dexterity.

Recommended fix small effort

Increase the target to at least 24×24 CSS pixels — usually by adding padding rather than changing the visual size of the icon — or ensure adequate spacing around it.

5 render-blocking resources delay first paint

12 pages 12 occurrences priority 55

5 stylesheets and scripts totalling 226.2 KB are requested before first paint.

How we know measured evidence
Render-blocking resources 5 Chromium network stack
Combined size 226.2 KB Chromium network stack
Measured FCP 868 ms Paint Timing API
/css/bootstrap.min.css 20.9 KB Chromium network stack
/js/jquery.fancybox.min.js 21.8 KB Chromium network stack
/js/lc_lightbox.lite.js 21.9 KB Chromium network stack

Why this matters interpretation

A stylesheet in the document head blocks rendering until it has downloaded and parsed, and a script without `async` or `defer` blocks HTML parsing entirely. Each of these resources therefore contributes directly to the delay before anything appears on screen. This rule is heuristic — it identifies resources requested early and large enough to matter, rather than reading the document structure — so verify against a DevTools trace before acting.

Impact: Users stare at a blank page for longer than necessary before any content appears.

Recommended fix medium effort

Add `defer` to scripts that do not need to run during parsing. Inline the critical CSS needed for above-the-fold content and load the remainder with a non-blocking pattern. Where a third-party stylesheet is blocking, self-host it or load it asynchronously.

Images are missing alt attributes

2 pages 23 occurrences WCAG 2.1 — 1.1.1 Non-text Content priority 50

16 image(s) have no `alt` attribute at all.

How we know measured evidence
Images without alt 16 DOM extraction
Total images on page 18 DOM extraction
Why this matters interpretation

An absent `alt` attribute is different from an empty one. `alt=""` declares the image decorative and screen readers skip it; a missing attribute leaves them nothing to work with, so most fall back to announcing the filename — which is rarely meaningful and often absurd.

Impact: Screen reader users lose whatever information the image carries. Search engines also lose the image-context signal.

Recommended fix small effort

Add `alt` text describing the image's purpose in context. For purely decorative images, use `alt=""` explicitly — the empty value is the correct declaration, not an omission.

Multiple pages share the same title

2 pages 2 occurrences priority 50

1 title(s) are used by more than one page, affecting 2 pages in total.

How we know measured evidence
Duplicated titles 1 Cross-page comparison
Pages affected 2 Cross-page comparison
Home - LG Soft India 2 pages Cross-page comparison
Why this matters interpretation

Titles are how search engines and users tell pages apart. When several pages carry the same title, search engines have difficulty deciding which is the best result for a query, and users looking at a list of results or browser tabs cannot distinguish them. This pattern almost always means a template is emitting a static title instead of interpolating page-specific content.

Impact: Weakened relevance signals and worse search presentation across a group of pages.

Recommended fix small effort

Make each title unique by interpolating page-specific content into the template — the product name, article headline, or category, plus the site name.

2 text resources are served uncompressed

1 page 1 occurrence priority 48

25.9 KB of text content is delivered without gzip or Brotli compression.

How we know measured evidence
Uncompressed resources 2 Content-Encoding response header
Current transfer size 25.9 KB Chromium network stack
Estimated size with Brotli 7.2 KB Estimated at ~72% reduction for text
/maps/api/js?key=%5Bredacted%5D&paint_origin=&libraries=geometry%2Csea… [truncated 91 chars] 13.4 KB Chromium network stack
/maps/vt?pb=%211m4%211m3%211i17%212i93821%213i60784%211m4%211m3%211i17… [truncated 844 chars] 12.4 KB Chromium network stack
Why this matters interpretation

No `Content-Encoding` header was present on these responses, meaning the server sent the raw bytes. Text compresses extremely well — typically 70–80% with Brotli — so this is one of the few optimisations that is both large and essentially free. The saving figure above is an estimate based on typical text compression ratios, not a measurement.

Impact: Roughly 18.6 KB of unnecessary transfer on every uncached page load, felt most on mobile connections.

Recommended fix trivial effort

Enable Brotli (with gzip fallback) for all text MIME types at the CDN or reverse proxy. This is usually a one-line configuration change in nginx, Cloudflare, or your hosting provider.

Why this matters interpretation

Console errors are usually written by application code that has already detected a problem and handled it — a failed request, a missing configuration value, a third-party script that did not load. They do not always break a user-visible feature, but each one marks a code path that did not do what its author intended.

Impact: Varies by cause. At minimum this indicates a degraded code path; at worst it is a feature failing quietly with the failure visible only to developers.

Recommended fix small effort

Trace the message to its source and decide whether it represents an expected condition (in which case it should not be logged at error level) or a genuine failure (in which case it should be fixed and monitored).

Links with no destination

12 pages 48 occurrences WCAG 2.1 — 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value priority 35

4 anchor element(s) have an empty, "#", or javascript: href.

How we know measured evidence
Anchors without a destination 4 DOM extraction
Example About Us DOM extraction
Why this matters interpretation

An anchor is a navigation element. When it carries no destination it is usually being used as a button with a JavaScript handler attached. That works for mouse users but breaks middle-click, right-click "open in new tab", and keyboard activation semantics, and it announces incorrectly to screen readers.

Impact: Keyboard and assistive-technology users get a control that announces as a link but does not behave like one. Mouse users lose open-in-new-tab.

Recommended fix trivial effort

Where the element performs an action rather than navigating, use `<button type="button">`. Where it does navigate, give it a real href so the browser can do its job.

How we know measured evidence

Why this matters interpretation

A canonical tag tells search engines which URL is authoritative when the same content is reachable at several addresses — with and without a trailing slash, with tracking parameters, over http and https. Without one, ranking signals can be split across duplicates rather than consolidated.

Impact: Potential duplicate-content dilution where the same page is reachable at multiple URLs.

Recommended fix small effort

Add a self-referencing `<link rel="canonical" href="…">` with the absolute preferred URL on every indexable page.

No X-Content-Type-Options header

13 pages 13 occurrences OWASP Secure Headers Project priority 32

The `x-content-type-options` response header is not set.

How we know measured evidence
Header x-content-type-options HTTP response headers
Present no HTTP response headers
Why this matters interpretation

Without `nosniff`, browsers may ignore the declared Content-Type and guess based on content. A user-uploaded file served as text/plain but containing HTML can then be interpreted as HTML and execute script.

Impact: This is a missing defence-in-depth control rather than an exploitable vulnerability on its own. It increases the damage another flaw could do.

Recommended fix small effort

Add `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`. It has essentially no compatibility risk.

No Referrer-Policy header

13 pages 13 occurrences OWASP Secure Headers Project priority 32

The `referrer-policy` response header is not set.

How we know measured evidence
Header referrer-policy HTTP response headers
Present no HTTP response headers
Why this matters interpretation

Without an explicit policy, browsers send the full URL of the current page — path and query string included — to third-party resources. Where URLs contain identifiers, reset tokens, or search terms, that is a quiet data leak to every analytics and ad domain on the page.

Impact: This is a missing defence-in-depth control rather than an exploitable vulnerability on its own. It increases the damage another flaw could do.

Recommended fix small effort

Add `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`. This keeps full referrer information for same-origin navigation while sending only the origin to third parties.

No clickjacking protection

13 pages 13 occurrences OWASP Secure Headers Project priority 32

The `x-frame-options` response header is not set.

How we know measured evidence
Header x-frame-options HTTP response headers
Present no HTTP response headers
Why this matters interpretation

Without `X-Frame-Options` or a CSP `frame-ancestors` directive, the page can be embedded in an invisible iframe on an attacker's site and overlaid with decoy controls, so a user believes they are clicking one thing while actually clicking another on your site.

Impact: This is a missing defence-in-depth control rather than an exploitable vulnerability on its own. It increases the damage another flaw could do.

Recommended fix small effort

Add `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN`, or preferably the modern equivalent `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'`.

350.9 KB of CSS is never used (96%)

12 pages 12 occurrences priority 22

96% of the CSS delivered to this page was never executed during load.

How we know measured evidence
Total CSS 366.9 KB Chromium coverage API
Unused 350.9 KB (96%) Chromium coverage API
/css/bootstrap.min.css 131.5 KB unused of 137.6 KB Chromium coverage API
/css/style.css 42.2 KB unused of 48.8 KB Chromium coverage API

/css/font-awesome.min.css 30.1 KB unused of 30.3 KB Chromium coverage API
Why this matters interpretation

Coverage measures CSS rules that matched no element on the page. Unused CSS still has to be downloaded and parsed, and a large stylesheet delays first paint because CSS is render-blocking. As with JavaScript, rules that apply only to other pages or to interactive states will appear unused in a single-page measurement.

Impact: Extra render-blocking bytes, which delays first paint.

Recommended fix medium effort

Split CSS per route or component, and inline only the critical above-the-fold rules in the document head with the rest loaded asynchronously.

No XML sitemap found

1 page 1 occurrence priority 17

No sitemap was found at /sitemap.xml, /sitemap_index.xml, or referenced from robots.txt.

How we know measured evidence
sitemap.xml not found HTTP probe
Referenced in robots.txt no robots.txt parse
Why this matters interpretation

A sitemap gives search engines an explicit list of URLs to crawl along with change frequency hints. Without one, crawlers rely entirely on following links — so pages that are poorly linked internally, or newly published, are discovered slowly or not at all.

Impact: Slower discovery and indexing of new or deeply-nested pages.

Recommended fix small effort

Generate an XML sitemap and reference it from robots.txt with a `Sitemap:` directive. Most frameworks and CMSs can produce one automatically.

No Permissions-Policy header

13 pages 13 occurrences OWASP Secure Headers Project priority 8

The `permissions-policy` response header is not set.

How we know measured evidence
Header permissions-policy HTTP response headers
Present no HTTP response headers
Why this matters interpretation

Permissions-Policy lets a site declare which powerful browser features (camera, microphone, geolocation, payment) may be used, including by embedded third-party frames. Without it, any embedded content can request those permissions in the site's name.

Impact: This is a missing defence-in-depth control rather than an exploitable vulnerability on its own. It increases the damage another flaw could do.

Recommended fix small effort

Add a Permissions-Policy disabling features the site does not use, e.g. `Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()`.

Method & Scope

What was tested

  • 13 page(s) loaded in a real Chromium browser at desktop viewport
  • 1362 network request(s) observed, 102.09 MB transferred
  • 52 interactive control(s) clicked and observed
  • 41 link target(s) verified · 1 broken
  • 1 console error(s) and uncaught exception(s) captured
  • Accessibility scanned with axe-core against WCAG 2.1 A/AA and 2.2 AA

How to read this report

  • Measured facts are observations from the browser. They are not estimates.
  • Interpretation is our reasoning from those facts, and is labelled separately.
  • Confidence — CONFIRMED means we observed the failure directly; POSSIBLE means the evidence is suggestive but a benign explanation exists.
  • Priority combines severity, confidence, how much of the site is affected, and effort.
  • AI enrichment was not used for this audit — all findings and prose are rule-generated.

Limits of this audit

  • Black-box only — no source code, backend, or database access.
  • Security checks are passive: response headers and transport configuration observed during normal page loads. No active scanning or probing was performed.
  • Interaction testing deliberately skips anything that looks destructive (delete, purchase, logout, submit), so those paths are untested.
  • Pages behind authentication were not tested.
  • A single measurement per page — network timing varies between runs.
  • 38 URL(s) were deliberately skipped (crawl traps, external hosts, non-page assets).
